quote: The laminar smoke point is the condition (and the luminous flame length) where a flame begins to emit soot.
subject: Definition of the laminar smoke point

quote: Fifty-two smoke points were found for ethylene, propane, propylene, and propylene/nitrogen mixtures.
subject: Number of smoke points found (abstract says 52; Table 1 adds to 52; closing remarks say 55; the datasheet lists 55)
conditions: Ethylene, propane, propylene and propylene/nitrogen mixtures; ISS.

quote: Burner diameters were 0.41, 0.76, and 1.6 mm and co-flow velocities varied from 5.4 – 65 cm/s.
subject: Range of burner diameters and co-flow velocities

quote: Increasing co-flow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths. Smaller burners have longer smoke points for co-flowing flames.
subject: Effect of co-flow velocity and burner size on flame length and smoke point

quote: The luminous flame lengths generally correlate with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction, although they increase slightly as air velocity decreases.
subject: Luminous flame length correlates with fuel mass flow rate divided by stoichiometric mixture fraction

quote: The measured smoke point lengths were found to correlate with burner diameter to the –0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power.
subject: Smoke point length scales as burner diameter to the -0.91 power times coflow velocity to the 0.41 power

quote: The measurements allow estimates of pseudo threshold soot indices (TSI) for microgravity diffusion flames, indicating an unusually high sooting propensity for propane in microgravity.
subject: Propane has an unusually high sooting propensity in microgravity

quote: Typical burn times were 60 s, and after each two such burns the MSG contents were flushed with ISS cabin air. The oxygen mole fraction of this cabin air is maintained within 19 – 24%.
subject: Burn time and the oxygen in the ISS cabin air used as the oxidizer
conditions: Oxygen mole fraction 19 to 24 percent (a range stated for the cabin air, not measured per test).

quote: The smoke point lengths, LSP, (and the flow conditions) were obtained from the video record and are the measured distance from the burner to the tip of the luminous flame on the flame axis.
subject: How the smoke point length was measured

quote: The luminous flame tips were not sharply defined in most images, but rather transitioned from bright yellow to black over an axial distance of 2 – 5 mm.
subject: Uncertainty in where the luminous flame tip is
conditions: Transition from bright yellow to black.

quote: Totally 526 flames were ignited and studied, which were much more than originally planned.
subject: Number of flames ignited in the flight tests

quote: The flames generally reached steady conditions within 5 s of ignition or a change in flow rate of fuel or air.
subject: Time for a flame to reach steady conditions
conditions: After ignition or after a change in fuel or air flow.

quote: Periodic flame motion was observed in some flames, especially those with high air velocity, large burners, and long flames, and is attributed to coflow perturbations.
subject: Periodic flame motion in some flames
conditions: High air velocity, large burners, long flames.

quote: Smoke points were attempted with methane, but could not be obtained before the flames impinged on the copper plate at the end of the duct.
subject: No methane smoke point was obtained
conditions: Methane flames reached the copper plate at the end of the duct before a smoke point was reached.

subject: Table 1: number of smoke points per fuel (C2H4, C3H8, C3H6, 75% C3H6, 50% C3H6)
conditions: Table 1, Summary of smoke points observed.

quote: Parameters ua, uf, and Re assume conditions of 298 K, 101 kPa and 21±1% O2, and uniform velocity profiles.
subject: Pressure, temperature and oxygen are assumed in the report's calculations, not measured

quote: For a given choice of fuel and burner diameter, an increase in coflow velocity generally increases the smoke point length.
subject: Smoke point length increases with coflow velocity
conditions: ISS, fixed fuel and burner diameter.

quote: Figure 18 reveals that smoke points of nonbuoyant coflowing flames decrease with increasing burner diameter.
subject: Smoke point length decreases with burner diameter

quote: The present smoke points generally were repeatable. An exception was the tests with the 0.41 mm burner (for which only propylene smoke points were possible). Testing on different days yielded different smoke points for this burner.
subject: Repeatability of smoke points; the 0.41 mm burner gave different smoke points on different days

quote: The sooting propensity of the present fuels, identified from the smoke point lengths for fixed burner diameter and coflow velocity, generally increases from propane to ethylene, to 50% propylene, to 75% propylene, and to propylene.
subject: Sooting propensity order as written on p. 16 of the report (propane lowest)
conditions: Contradicts the closing remarks (ethylene lowest); the next sentence on the page gives an exception for the 0.76 mm burner.

quote: The only exception was that, for the 0.76 mm burner, ethylene has a longer smoke point length than propane. The lower density of ethylene results in a decreased residence time, but this is unlikely to explain such a long smoke point relative to that of propane.
subject: Ethylene has a longer smoke point than propane for the 0.76 mm burner

quote: Smoke points of 55 microgravity gas-jet diffusion flames in coflowing air were measured in earth orbit.
subject: Number of smoke points measured (closing remarks)

quote: The sooting propensities of the present fuel mixtures in microgravity increase according to ethylene < propane < 50% propylene < 75% propylene < propylene. This is the same as in normal gravity except for the exchanged positions of ethylene and propane.
subject: Sooting propensity order in microgravity (closing remarks)
